text:
For a diagnostic preserving one-negative training, average 99 baseline-equivalent pair losses: BCE = softplus(−s₊) + meanⱼ softplus(sⱼ); BPR = meanⱼ softplus(sⱼ−s₊). Preserve the baseline’s exact normalization, valid-position masking and example weights, including any factor ½. By linearity, this preserves expected loss and gradient when negatives follow the original distribution; uniform sampling without replacement preserves that expectation despite dependence. If sampling differs, use importance weights p₀(j)/q(j) for independent draws, or inclusion-probability weighting for unique samples. Match exclusion rules and support; self-normalized weights generally introduce bias. These are mathematical consequences of averaging the [standard loss definitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07770).

Joint BCE over one positive plus 99 negatives, averaged over 100 labels, changes positive:negative weighting from 1:1 to 1:99; summing instead also changes gradient scale. Neither preserves the baseline objective. Joint sampled softmax couples candidates through a shared denominator and changes gradients; only uncorrected two-candidate softmax equals BPR. Full-catalog softmax approximations require sampling corrections—typically negative logits adjusted by −log(Kq(j)) for independent draws, with inclusion probabilities for unique samples and the deterministic positive handled separately. Corrections generally retain finite-sample gradient bias; they do not recover one-negative BCE/BPR. See [sampled-softmax analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.09331v1).

[gSASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07192) attributes BCE overconfidence to inflated positive prevalence under negative sampling; it combines more negatives with generalized BCE to mitigate this. That mechanism differs from easy-negative saturation: BCE negative-logit gradients are sigmoid(sⱼ), while BPR uses sigmoid(sⱼ−s₊). Diagnose their distributions and hard-negative tails alongside baseline-equivalent averaged gradients; negative-count changes alone do not establish saturation or miscalibration.
